title: Protesters Challenge Trump’s Proposed Arch Near Washington Landmarks
summary:
Dozens of people gathered at Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, October 1, 2026, to protest a large arch proposed by President Donald Trump. The planned structure would stand 250 feet tall in a traffic circle on the bridge connecting the National Mall to Arlington National Cemetery.

Veterans, retirees and lawmakers attended the protest. Speakers questioned the arch’s size, cost and location, as well as its lack of congressional approval. They stood beside a model made from a tarp, which they said was much smaller than the proposed monument.

Jon Gundersen, a retired Army veteran and former Foreign Service officer, traveled from South Carolina to attend. He is among the Vietnam War veterans suing the administration over the project. Public Citizen, a group leading that lawsuit, helped organize the protest.

Several speakers said veterans and their families should have more input into the plans. Senator Tammy Duckworth and other opponents argued that improving services for veterans would be a better way to honor them.

The White House has offered a different view. It told NPR that the arch would improve visits to the cemetery and serve as a reminder of American heroes’ sacrifices.

The proposal is still moving through federal approval steps. Administration officials told historic preservation groups at a Tuesday meeting that they planned to continue with the original arch proposal. The National Capital Planning Commission is widely expected to consider it at its meeting in early November.

A separate review concerning nearby protected landmarks ended early in the last week of September. The Advisory Council on Historic Preservation said it would send recommendations directly to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum by October 7. Charles Birnbaum of The Cultural Landscape Foundation criticized the decision to end discussions after only two meetings.

Some protesters hope Congress will block federal funding for the arch. An attempt by Democrats to do so was blocked by a Republican senator earlier that week. November’s midterm elections could change which party holds power in Congress, potentially affecting the project starting in January. For now, the lawsuit continues and final federal approval remains pending.
why_it_matters: The dispute connects a proposed monument with veterans’ input, public spending, congressional authority and protection of nearby landmarks. Ongoing legal and federal review processes leave the project’s future undecided.
